summary:
A solar flare is coming, and two of your astronauts are outside. Do you send everyone to the shelter, or keep working?

We built Outpost Commander: Moon & Mars, a free browser game for kids aged 7–12. You run a base on the Moon or Mars. Every day you share out limited power between life support, heaters, the lab and machines, give your crew jobs, end the day, and read a Day Report that explains every result and its cause.

The game makes the challenge's trade-offs real: life support, radiation shielding, power budgeting and food production all compete for the same power and crew time. Events come from real NASA missions, like the 1972 solar storm and the dust storm that ended the Opportunity rover, with a NASA source for each fact.

This matters because kids learn the core idea behind real missions by playing: every choice has a cost, and today's decision shapes tomorrow. Next mission, they plan ahead.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Outpost Commander: Moon & Mars is a browser game where kids aged 7–12 run a base on the Moon or Mars. Each mission starts with packing a rocket that can only lift 100 tonnes, so every tonne of batteries is a tonne less of food or building materials. On the surface, every day has four steps:

1. Share out power between life support, heaters, the science lab and machines.

2. Give the four crew members jobs: research, mining, collecting ice, building, exploring, repairing or resting.

3. End the day.

4. Read the Day Report, which shows every change and its cause, for example "Solar flare, inside the storm shelter (85% blocked) +7.2 mSv".

Events force real decisions. When a solar flare warning appears, you choose: send everyone into the storm shelter, or keep working. In our test, sheltering added 8 mSv of radiation. Keeping two astronauts outside added 49 mSv, a third of the crew's whole limit, for a few extra science points. On the Moon, 6-day nights switch solar panels off. On Mars, dust storms cut solar power to 20%. Kids learn to plan ahead: charge batteries before dark, build soil shielding before the Sun acts up.

BENEFITS

- Free, runs in any modern browser on a laptop or phone, no login or install.

- A guided first mission, a suggested rocket kit and an autopilot help younger players start.

- Every result is explained, so kids see why things happened, not just whether they won.

- Each in-game fact links to its NASA or JPL source (about 80 links).

INTENDED IMPACT

We want kids to understand the core idea behind real missions: resources are limited, every choice has a cost, and today's decision shapes tomorrow. The game can be played at home or used as a classroom mission exercise. Our next step is to test it with a class and see whether kids change their plan on the second try.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

- HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no game engine or framework.

- Graphics drawn in code with SVG and CSS. Sound made with the Web Audio API.

- Progress saved in the browser (localStorage). After loading, the game makes no further network calls.

- Fonts: Barlow and Barlow Condensed (Google Fonts).

- Hosted on Netlify.

- Claude (Anthropic) helped us build the game and create the presentation and project text.

CREATIVITY

Instead of quizzing kids on facts, the game puts them in the commander's seat at the moment a real danger hits. The science appears when it matters: the flare warning shows the real August 1972 solar storm that struck between Apollo 16 and 17. The Day Report turns abstract trade-offs into visible numbers a child can follow.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Age 7–12: short sentences, icons paired with words, the same four steps every day.

- Accuracy vs. playability: events are based on real NASA missions and measurements, such as Curiosity's radiation data, Opportunity's dust storm and MOXIE's oxygen. Values like the 150 mSv limit and the 85% shelter protection are simplified for play, and the game says so.

- Replay value: 13 locations, random events, mission goals, upgrades, badges and a daily challenge.

- Access: works on low-cost devices and phones, sound can be turned off, and the game respects the "reduce motion" setting.
